demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again
I remind myself it could have been worse
I dwell on what I have done wrong

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I feel isolated and set apart from others
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm as a coping strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only markedly high-risk/impulsive strategy and is poorly supported by the rest of the selected nodes. The other strategies are comparatively cognitive/obsessional (mental rituals, downward comparison), and the threat/memory/appraisal items do not show the broader dysregulation, dissociation, or severe affective overload that would make this combination clinically cohesive.

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Pain recall implies the patient was physically injured in the traumatic event. That is hard to reconcile with the trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another' unless she was also injured, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. The rest of the memory items emphasize fragmented retrieval and sensory reliving, but not a personally injured trauma narrative.

vignette:
Amina, a 47-year-old African American architect, came to treatment after months of living as though she had stepped out of her own life and into someone else's. The event she kept circling back to had happened during a routine site visit to a downtown renovation project. A temporary barrier had been left in place, a worker had been nearby, and in a split second of misjudgment she gave instructions that led to a serious injury. She did not describe the scene in a dramatic way; what made it unbearable was how ordinary it had been before it went wrong. Since then, she had been certain that somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, and that belief had hardened into a private verdict on her character. That conviction kept drawing her back to the moment itself, as if she had to review it again and again to locate where she had failed; the more she told herself she should have seen it coming, the more vividly the scene returned, heavy with the sense that she was permanently changed. She compared herself bitterly with the person she used to be, a competent, careful woman her colleagues trusted, and the person she had become felt unrecognisable to her. What frightened her most was not only what had happened, but what it seemed to say about her: that she was the kind of person who could harm others through carelessness and then have to live with it.

In the weeks after the accident, Amina found that trying to think about it directly was like reaching for something submerged and losing her grip. When she tried to deliberately remember, she could not access the memory in a clear, orderly way, yet pieces of it burst in without warning: the taste in her mouth during the incident returned with unsettling vividness, and sometimes she heard fragments of what had been said at the scene echoing in her head. Those intrusions made her feel as if the danger were still active, and she had learned to answer them by keeping the television on late, by staying busy on purpose, and by repeating silent phrases before bed so the images would not gather in the quiet. Those involuntary flashes made the event feel less past than present, and they fed the sense that danger was still close by. She began to react as if she were in danger even when nothing was actually wrong, flinching at ordinary sounds in her office or at home, especially sudden beeps, dropped tools, or a slammed door in the street below her apartment. The memory's broken, sensory quality also deepened her self-judgment; each flash seemed to prove that she had not simply been unlucky, but fundamentally at fault. As she put it, the memory itself kept showing her the worst moment of her life, and that made it easier to conclude that she had no one to blame but herself.

Over time, Amina developed a set of private routines meant to keep bad things from happening again. She performed mental rituals before driving to a job site, before answering difficult emails, and before going to sleep, repeating phrases in her head as if precision of thought could prevent another catastrophe. She also caught herself dwelling on what she had done wrong for hours at a time, turning the scene over and over in search of the exact mistake she believed must be hidden somewhere inside it. At moments when the guilt grew unbearable, she reminded herself that it could have been worse, that the worker had survived, that others had suffered more. But even that comparison did not soothe her for long; it was less comfort than a brief attempt to keep herself from falling apart. The more she leaned on these rituals and self-reassurances, the more they seemed to keep the memory alive. Trying not to think about the event made it return in sharper flashes, and each return renewed the startle, the sense of threat, and the conviction that she had become someone dangerous and separate from other people. On the nights when she felt most on edge, the memory came back most easily, pulled loose by the very feeling of danger she was trying to outrun; and because she had spent so long warding it off, it remained undiminished, almost as vivid as when it happened. The pattern tightened until she found herself guarding against imagined disaster all day, while the very acts meant to control it left her more haunted and more certain that she was isolated and set apart.

At work, this cycle had begun to change how she functioned. On site visits she avoided standing near open edges, machinery, or anything that could jolt her attention, and in meetings she struggled to concentrate long enough to follow detailed discussions. Each time she relied on these safety habits to get through a site visit, they seemed to confirm the thought she could not shake: that she was not coping the way other people did, and that the only reason she could keep going at all was by arranging her day around what frightened her. She became more inward with her colleagues, less willing to speak casually, as if distance might protect them from her and protect her from being seen too clearly. Even at home, with her husband asking simple questions over dinner, she would sometimes go blank for a moment after an ordinary noise from outside, then excuse herself and retreat to the bathroom to steady her breathing and repeat the same silent phrases. The downward comparison returned there too: she reminded herself that it could have been worse, but the thought always circled back to the same place, to what she had done and what it had made of her. By the time she sought help, Amina was exhausted by the constant vigilance, the intrusive fragments of sound and taste, and the rituals she felt compelled to perform. She came because she was afraid the loop would never stop, and because beneath the shame and isolation there remained a guarded hope that she might still find a way back to the woman she had once recognized as herself.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not clearly show her negative beliefs causing the memory to occur or intensify in the same paragraph.
It does not explicitly state that the intrusive memory drives her to use the maladaptive rituals or avoidance strategies.
No paragraph clearly states that her sense of threat leads to the memory intruding or being reactivated.
No paragraph clearly states that feeling threatened causes her negative appraisals to worsen.
The vignette says the rituals keep the memory alive, but it does not clearly show the maladaptive strategies causing the memory itself in a causal way.
The vignette says the rituals leave her more haunted and isolated, but it does not clearly show the maladaptive strategies producing the negative appraisals as a causal outcome.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not clearly show her negative beliefs causing the memory to occur or intensify in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: It does not explicitly state that the intrusive memory drives her to use the maladaptive rituals or avoidance strategies.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Threat → Memory: No paragraph clearly states that her sense of threat leads to the memory intruding or being reactivated.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph clearly states that feeling threatened causes her negative appraisals to worsen.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: The vignette says the rituals keep the memory alive, but it does not clearly show the maladaptive strategies causing the memory itself in a causal way.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: The vignette says the rituals leave her more haunted and isolated, but it does not clearly show the maladaptive strategies producing the negative appraisals as a causal outcome.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
